property_summary: After a successful lockInGuess call by any account with 1 ether, the stored guesses[address].block is strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was called (i.e., records next block); the mutant that records the current block violates this for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether, the recorded guesses[msg.sender].block is strictly greater than the block.number at the time of the call (i.e., the contract records the next block); the mutant that records the current block will sometimes record a block number equal to the current block, violating this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the contract records a nonzero block number strictly greater than the block number at which the call executed (i.e., it records next block); the mutant that records the current block can record a block number equal to the current block for some input, violating this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the contract records a stored block number strictly greater than the block number at call time (records next block); the mutant that records the current block can record a block number equal to the current block, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the stored guesses[caller].block is nonzero and strictly greater than the block number at which the call returned (i.e., the contract records the next block); the mutant that records block.number (current block) can make the stored block equal to the current block, violating the strict > relation for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the contract records the pending block number equal to current block.number + 1; the mutant that sets it to block.number + 2 will violate this for some fuzzed block numbers (the recorded block differs).

After a successful lockInGuess by any caller sending exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the stored guesses(caller).block equals block.number + 1 in the correct contract for every input; the mutant that sets it to block.number + 2 will make that equality fail for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the contract records guesses(caller).block equal to the current block.number + 1; the mutant that sets it to block.number + 2 violates this for some inputs.

After any successful lockInGuess(call) by an address sending exactly 1 ether when they have no prior guess, the stored guesses(address).block always equals block.number + 1 (reference) — the mutant that stores block.number + 2 breaks this equality for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess sending exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the contract records guesses(caller).block equal to block.number + 1; the mutant that stores block.number + 2 will sometimes make that recorded block differ from block.number + 1 (the fuzzer will find such a case).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the stored guesses(addr).block in the correct contract equals the block number at call time plus one; the mutant that writes a constant 1 breaks this rule for callers when block.number+1 != 1 (i.e. almost always).

After a successful lockInGuess by any caller paying 1 ether with no prior guess, the stored guesses[caller].block equals the current block.number + 1 for all admissible inputs; the mutant that stores a constant 1 instead will cause this to be false for many inputs (e.g. when block.number + 1 != 1).

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether with no prior guess, the contract stores guesses[caller].block equal to block.number + 1; the mutant that writes a constant 1 breaks this because it sets the stored block to 1 instead of block.number + 1 for many block numbers.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the stored guesses[caller].block is nonzero and not equal to 1 if the current block.number+1 != 1; the mutant that always writes 1 will make stored block equal to 1 for some inputs where block.number+1 != 1, violating the property.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess paying exactly 1 ether with no prior guess, the stored guesses[caller].block equals the block number at the time of the call plus one; the mutant that sets the stored block to constant 1 will violate this when block.number + 1 != 1.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the stored guesses[msg.sender].block must be nonzero and strictly greater than the stored guesses[msg.sender].block minus zero and the stored guesses[msg.sender].guess must equal the provided hash; the mutant that swaps assignments can transiently make guess unset when subsequent external actions (like inspecting the mapping) are observed immediately after the call — specifically, the reference always stores the provided guess value for the caller after lockInGuess, while the mutant can leave guess unset when racey/ordering sensitive observation is made (fuzzer finds inputs that distinguish stored guess equality).

After a caller successfully calls lockInGuess paying 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the contract must record the provided guess bytes32 value for that caller (guesses[msg.sender].guess == suppliedHash); the mutant that assigns block before guess can be distinguished because a reentrant attacker can call back into settle (or otherwise exploit ordering) to observe a different stored guess value, causing the property to fail for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether and had no prior guess, the contract must immediately record the provided bytes32 guess in the public mapping getter; the mutant that assigns block before guess can be broken by a reentrant attacker that calls settle during lockInGuess, leaving the stored guess unset for some inputs.

For any caller who pays exactly 1 ether to lockInGuess when they have no prior guess, after the call the contract's public mapping must report that guesses(caller).guess equals the supplied hash; the mutant that assigns block before guess can be reentrancy-exploited to leave the stored guess not equal to the supplied hash for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether when they had no prior guess, the contract must record guesses[caller].guess == suppliedHash after the call; the mutant that assigns block before guess can be exploited by a reentrant helper (whose fallback calls settle) to make the stored guess differ and thus violate this rule for some inputs.
Calling settle when the caller has no active guess must revert (i.e., settle does not silently return on missing guess).

For any address that locked a guess for a future block, calling settle will only succeed in paying out if the blockhash of the locked block equals the guess; using block.number instead (mutant) can erroneously make settle compare against the current blockhash and thus sometimes pay out (or behave differently) when the original would not — so the property: after a lockInGuess for block N, calling settle in block N+1 never results in address(c).balance decreasing (i.e., no payout) for the reference when the guess did not match the locked blockhash, while the mutant can produce a payout for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess for block B with a guessed bytes32 that does NOT equal blockhash(B), calling settle after B (in some later block) never decreases address(c).balance in the correct contract; the mutant that uses block.number instead of the locked block can (for some fuzzed inputs and timing) pay out erroneously, decreasing address(c).balance.

For any caller who locked a guess for block B with some bytes32 guess, calling settle in a later block never causes the contract balance to decrease in the correct contract when the guess does not equal blockhash(B); the mutant using block.number can cause an unexpected payout (balance decrease) for some fuzzed inputs/timings.

For any caller who locks a guess for a specific future block with a guess that is unequal to the blockhash of that locked block, settling after that locked block must never transfer funds out of the contract (contract balance stays the same); the mutant that reads blockhash(block.number) can sometimes match the guess against the current blockhash and erroneously pay out, decreasing the contract balance.

For any caller who locked a guess for a future block with some bytes32 guess, if the locked-block's blockhash is zero (i.e. the locked block is too old/unavailable) then the reference contract will never pay out on settle (settle will not decrease address(c).balance), while the mutant that uses block.number might observe a nonzero current blockhash and (for some fuzzed inputs/timings) incorrectly pay out — so the invariant: when the stored locked block's blockhash == 0, calling settle never transfers funds out in the correct contract, but the mutant can transfer funds for some inputs.

For any caller who previously locked a guess that equals the blockhash of the recorded block, settle pays out 2 ether only when the stored guess equals the actual blockhash (which can be zero), but the mutant makes success depend on a fixed nonzero constant so there exist inputs (a stored guess not equal to that constant but equal to the real blockhash) where reference may pay and mutant will not; thus after settle the contract balance in reference can decrease for some fuzzed guess/block timing while mutant's balance stays unchanged.

For any caller who locked a guess (a bytes32) for a future block, calling settle either leaves C's balance unchanged or transfers 2 ether to that caller if and only if the stored guess equals the actual blockhash at the recorded block; the mutant replacing blockhash with a fixed nonzero constant breaks this by making payout depend on equality with that constant instead, so there exist fuzzed guesses/blocks where the reference can pay but the mutant will not (observed via address(c).balance).

For any caller who locked a nonzero guess hash and waited until after the target block, calling settle on the correct contract will never pay out when the stored guess is zero, but the mutant can incorrectly pay out only when the stored guess equals a fixed nonzero constant; thus the invariant: after lockInGuess with guess == bytes32(0), settle never reduces the contract balance (no payout) — the reference preserves this for all inputs, but the mutant might violate it if it treats a fixed nonzero constant as the answer (which cannot equal zero), so the mutant does not violate in this exact case; to distinguish we instead rely on the general rule that if a caller locks bytes32(0) it can never ever win on the reference (because blockhash can be zero but equality prevents payout when guess==0), while the mutant might also never win — to find a distinguishing input we instead use a different invariant: if a caller locks any guess that is equal to blockhash of the recorded block, settle on the reference will succeed (contract balance decreases) exactly when that equality holds; the mutant replaces blockhash with a fixed constant so there exist fuzzed guess values equal to the real blockhash that will cause the reference to pay but the mutant not to — we express this by fuzzing the guess and the block number and asserting that for all guesses that equal blockhash(recordedBlock) the reference's settle reduces contract balance (payout), which the mutant breaks for some fuzzed inputs.

For any caller who locked a guess equal to the blockhash of the recorded block, calling settle will transfer 2 ether to that caller (reducing address(c).balance); the mutant that replaces blockhash with a fixed nonzero constant breaks this because there exist fuzzed guesses/blocks where the real blockhash equals the stored guess but differs from the constant, so the reference pays and the mutant does not.

For any caller who locked a guess equal to the blockhash of the recorded block, calling settle on the correct contract will always pay out 2 ether (reducing address(c).balance) — the mutant that replaces blockhash with a fixed nonzero constant can fail to pay for some such guesses, breaking this rule.

For any caller who locked a guess, after calling settle the reference contract always clears the stored guess.block (so address(c).balance decreases by 2 ether on a successful match and the stored block becomes zero); the mutant that defers clearing until after transfer can leave the stored block non-zero if the transfer reverts, causing different observable state (settle caller's recorded block remains non-zero and funds stay in contract).

For any caller who locked a guess and then calls settle, the reference contract always clears the caller's stored guesses[caller].block (making its getter return 0) after settle completes; the mutant that clears the block only after attempting the payout can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the transfer to the caller fails, so the mutant can violate this rule for some inputs (a failing recipient).

For every caller who locked a guess and then calls settle, the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block (making its public getter return 0) when settle returns; the mutant that defers clearing until after transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero if the payout to the caller reverts (e.g., the caller is a reverting contract), so the mutant violates this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller who previously locked a guess, after they invoke settle() the reference contract always clears their stored guesses[caller].block to 0 regardless of whether sending Ether to them succeeds; the mutant that clears the block only after the transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero when the transfer to the caller reverts, thus violating this invariant.

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle(), the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 when settle returns; the mutant that defers clearing until after transfer can leave guesses[caller].block non-zero if sending Ether to the caller reverts (so a reverting recipient breaks this rule).

For any caller who locked a guess, calling settle in a later block (block.number > lockedBlock) always clears their stored guess entry (block becomes 0) in the correct contract; the mutant that allows settle in the same block can clear the entry earlier (when block.number == lockedBlock) causing different post-settle storage, so there exist inputs (calls settled in the lock-in block) that make the mutant violate this rule.

After a successful lockInGuess by an address, if settle is called in a strictly later block the contract always clears that address's stored block to 0; the mutant that permits settle in the same block can clear the stored block prematurely when settle is invoked in the same block as lockInGuess (breaking the invariant for some inputs).

For any address that locked a guess, calling settle in a strictly later block must always clear that address's stored guess.block to 0 after the call; the mutant that allows settling in the same block can clear the stored block when settle is invoked in the same block as lockInGuess, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any address that has locked a guess, calling settle in a later block (block.number > lockedBlock) always leaves the contract's balance decreased by 0 or 2 ether depending on match but — crucially — calling settle in the same block as lockInGuess must NOT be admissible; we instead restrict to only allow settle calls from a different address than the locker in the same block so that the reference always keeps the locker entry untouched until a later block, while the mutant that permits settle in the same block can clear the locker entry prematurely when the same locker calls settle in the lock-in block; the test enforces admissible domain (settle called by the locker) and asserts that after settle in the SAME block the stored guess.block remains nonzero for the reference but is cleared by the mutant (the mutant thus violates this rule for some input).

For any address that has just called lockInGuess in block B, calling settle in the same block B must revert (i.e., not be allowed) on the correct contract, but the mutant (which uses >=) allows settle to proceed in the same block and thus will not revert for some inputs.
